links.note: Greek has no word for “the” here: ἀρχῇ stands alone.
Greek says “the God”; English drops the article.
Greek puts θεὸς first: “God was the Word.” English moves it to the end.
The Greek says “not even one.”
Greek says “to him”; English turns this into “whose.”
English supplies “was sent” to complete the contrast.
English supplies “Son” for the Greek adjective used as a noun.
Greek says “has come before me”; English expresses this as surpassing.
Greek uses a preposition meaning “in place of.”
English recasts “so we may give an answer” as a request.
Greek says “we may give”; English phrases this as taking the answer back.
The Greek participle means “those who had been sent.”
English combines “asked and said” into “asked.”
English combines “answered, saying” into one verb.
The Greek verb’s ending carries the subject “he.”
The Greek relative and particle express “whomever.”
Greek joins John and the disciples with “and”; English uses “with.”
Greek uses a participle: Jesus is walking.
English adds “and” when turning the participles into separate actions.
Greek says “heard from John.”
The Greek article’s dative case locates this on the following day.
English adds “him” before the relative clause.
Greek says “be”; English renders the question with “come.”
English combines “answered and said” into “answered.”
English combines “answered and said” into “answered.”
